title: How Egypt Learned to Speak Again
paragraphs: For centuries, the carved signs on Egyptian temples were a mystery. Visitors stared at the walls without understanding a single word. Nobody could read hieroglyphs, and the language behind them had been forgotten. That changed after French soldiers working in Egypt in seventeen ninety nine discovered a slab of dark stone near the town of Rosetta.

The stone carried one decree written in three scripts: hieroglyphs, a simpler Egyptian script known as Demotic, and ancient Greek. Scholars could read Greek, so they realised that the other two versions must say the same thing. This comparison gave them their first real clues. After the French surrender, the stone passed to Britain, and it has been displayed in the British Museum since eighteen oh two.

Decipherment was not quick, however. Researchers such as Thomas Young made early progress, but it was the French scholar Jean-Francois Champollion who announced in eighteen twenty two that he had cracked the system. He showed that many signs stood for sounds, not just for ideas. Ancient Egypt could finally speak in its own words. Today, scholars can read many Egyptian texts written on stone and papyrus.

sources.claim: Taş 1799'da Mısır'da Fransız askerlerce Rosetta yakınında bulundu; aynı ferman hiyeroglif, Demotik ve Yunanca olmak üzere üç yazıyla yazılıydı.
